title: He Was Clinically Blind on One Side, Yet Pointed to Lights 90% Right

acts.name: London 1974: Pitch-Dark Left Field Yet Uncanny Pointing
sentences: Blind on his left, Patient D.B. swore half the room went dark!
Yet when doctors flashed a dot there, he pointed right at it!
That real case was Lawrence Weiskrantz's Patient D.B.
Asked to point anyway — his finger landed dead-on!
In nineteen seventy-four, London doctors witnessed that shock.
Brain surgery in London saved young Patient D.B.'s life.
Yet it removed his right primary visual cortex, the vision center.
All left of his nose vanished into blankness.
Things turned with textbook rules of sight.

acts.name: Weiskrantz's 'Just Guess' Test & 90% Blind Accuracy
sentences: Lawrence Weiskrantz and Elizabeth Warrington tested him in London.
Both eyes and pupils stayed fully healthy.
Flashing light into his left side drew silence.
He flagged nothing at all on each trial.
Then Weiskrantz asked him to reach and guess.
He pointed at dots ninety percent right, like nine of ten!
On X or O cards, he hit ninety percent, like clockwork!
Laughing in disbelief, he thought he failed each try!
Blind inside yet pointing true was a total nightmare.

acts.name: Ancient Reflex Detour: 10% Eye Fibers Bypass Main Screen
sentences: How could darkness guide an accurate hand?
Ninety percent of eye wires, like nine of ten lanes, hit back cortex.
When surgery removed that wall, conscious pictures vanished.
Yet ten percent of the optic nerve — eye cable — branches early!
Those fibers dive straight into the brainstem — your reflex center.
A shortcut hops across the thalamus — your sensory relay station.
Ancient fish and frogs steered lives with that path!
Your reflex map tracks motion without sense.
Could someone fully walk through a crowded hall?

acts.name: Single-Screen Camera Myth vs Emotional Blindsight
sentences: People assume vision works like one screen screen.
Smash the main screen, and each visual skill should die.
Skeptics claimed stray room light explained those London guesses.
Controls with dimmed rooms crushed the stray-light excuse.
In two thousand eight, Beatrice de Gelder tested blindness.
Two strokes had wiped out both back hemispheres fully.
Without a cane, Patient T.N. saw zero shapes or edges.
What happened when the team filled a hallway with obstacles?

acts.name: 2008 Obstacle Hallway Walk Without One Bump Climax
sentences: The team scattered chairs, boxes, and tripods down a corridor.
They asked the walker to stroll straight ahead.
Without one cane tap, he weaved past each chair!
His shoulders angled sideways through narrow box gaps cleanly.
He crossed the obstacle course with zero collisions!
Shown faces on screen, your alarm matched smiles!
That study changed psychology overnight.
Instead of one screen, two vision streams run inside you.

acts.name: Flinching Before Seeing & Trusting Quiet Reflexes
sentences: Have you felt your reflex sight?
Ever duck a fast ball before naming it?
Your reflex shortcut flinches milliseconds faster than a blink!
Conscious pictures arrive moments after your hand moves.
Guessing drills train spared pathways.
Sight is richer than the picture you narrate.
Beneath sense, ancient guardian circuits watch each step.
That biological lesson explains why gut sight moves before thought.

full_script: Clinically blind on his left side, Patient D.B. swore half the room was pitch dark! Then his doctor flashed a silent dot into that dark half. Patient D.B. insisted he saw nothing at all. Asked to point anyway — his finger landed dead-on! In nineteen seventy-four, London doctors witnessed that exact shock. Brain surgery in London saved young Patient D.B.'s life. Yet it removed his right primary visual cortex, the vision center. Everything left of his nose vanished into blankness. Inside the room, things turned with textbook rules of sight. Lawrence Weiskrantz and Elizabeth Warrington tested him in London. Both eyes and pupils stayed completely healthy. Flashing light into his blind left side drew silence. He reported nothing at all on every trial. Then Weiskrantz asked him simply to reach and guess. His hand pointed to unseen targets ninety percent right, like nine of ten coins! Shown giant X or O shapes, he guessed ninety percent again, like an ace! Laughing in disbelief, he thought he failed every try! Blind inside yet pointing true — for him, this was a total nightmare. How could blind darkness guide an accurate human hand? Ninety percent of eye wires, like nine of ten lanes, hit back cortex. When surgery removed that wall, conscious pictures vanished. Yet ten percent of the optic nerve — the eye cable — branches off early! Those older fibers dive straight into the brainstem — your reflex center. Another shortcut hops across the thalamus — your sensory relay station. Ancient fish and frogs steered whole lives with that path! Your reflex map tracks motion without waking awareness. Could someone completely blind walk through a crowded hall? People assume human vision works like one television screen. Smash the main screen, and every visual skill should die. Skeptics claimed stray room light explained those London guesses. Careful controls with dimmed rooms crushed the stray-light excuse. In two thousand eight, Beatrice de Gelder tested total blindness. Two strokes had wiped out both back hemispheres completely. Without a cane, Patient T.N. saw zero shapes or edges. What happened when researchers filled a long hallway with obstacles? Researchers scattered chairs, boxes, and tripods down a corridor. They asked the blind walker simply to stroll straight ahead. Without one cane tap, he weaved past every chair! His shoulders angled sideways through narrow box gaps cleanly. He crossed the entire obstacle course with zero collisions! Shown faces on screen, his emotional alarm even matched smiles! Changed psychology overnight Instead of one screen, two parallel vision streams run inside you. Have you felt your hidden reflex sight? Ever duck a fast ball before naming it? Your reflex shortcut flinches milliseconds faster than a blink! Conscious pictures arrive moments after your hand moves. In stroke clinics, guessing drills train spared pathways. Sight is richer than the picture you narrate. Beneath awareness, ancient guardian circuits watch every step. That single finding explains why your eyes know more than your mind admits.
